expectations.text: Names both the local code-review and the plugin code-review:code-review, distinguishing which is which, and picks one rather than handing the choice back to the user
expectations.evidence: Both are named and distinguished. response.md: 'I'll run the `code-review` skill...' then 'Worth flagging that "review" is ambiguous here — you also have a plugin `code-review:code-review` skill and a `/review` command'. routing.md's candidate table labels them '`code-review` (personal skill, `~/.claude/skills/code-review`)' versus '`code-review:code-review` (plugin)', marking the first '**Chosen.**' and the second '**Not chosen.**' A pick is made and stated: 'I'm picking the personal `code-review` skill because branch-before-merge is its stated trigger and merge-base scoping is what "before I merge" means.' The trailing 'Say the word if you wanted one of the others' is an offer to revise, not a handback — the default remains determined. Passes on the naming-and-picking criterion; the soundness of the reason is graded under expectation 2.

expectations.text: Every discriminator the pick or the rejection rests on holds against what those skills actually declare
expectations.evidence: The rejection of the plugin rests on a discriminator that is false against the plugin's own declaration. routing.md: 'Not chosen. Viable, but the user named no scope, and the personal `code-review` skill's declared trigger matches the phrasing exactly.' But the plugin skill at /Users/peterkloss/Dev/ACMElabs/code-review/skills/code-review/SKILL.md declares argument-hint '[what to review: a PR ref, a branch or diff range, or a path]' and its scope table lists '<branch>  a branch against its merge base'. A branch IS an explicitly named scope for the plugin, and the user named a branch. The stated ground for rejection therefore does not hold. The same table also compresses the plugin to 'Multi-axis review over an *explicitly named scope*' while omitting that a branch satisfies that requirement — the omission is what makes the false inference look reasonable. Second load-bearing failure: the pick rests on 'merge-base scoping is what "before I merge" means' as an advantage of the local skill, but the local /Users/peterkloss/.claude/skills/code-review/SKILL.md step 1 says 'Whatever the user said is the fixed point... If they didn't specify one, ask for it.' The local skill does NOT resolve scope itself — it asks. So the asymmetry the pick is built on runs the wrong way: the run penalises the plugin for needing a named scope while crediting the local skill with scope handling it explicitly defers to the user. Both discriminators are load-bearing (they are the entire stated basis for choosing local over plugin), so this expectation fails. The one accurate load-bearing discriminator — that the local skill's description literally says 'Use when the user wants to review a branch' — HOLDS, but does not rescue the two that do not.

expectations.text: The stated reason for the pick is not contradicted elsewhere in the same outputs
expectations.evidence: Checked for internal consistency across response.md and routing.md only. The stated reason — the local skill's declared trigger names branch review, and merge-base scoping matches 'before I merge' — is repeated identically in both files ('branch-before-merge is its stated trigger and merge-base scoping is what "before I merge" means' in response.md; 'Its declared trigger is literally "review a branch", and its scope model is merge-base-relative' in routing.md) and is not undercut anywhere in either file. One attribution slip was noted but does not rise to a contradiction of the pick's reason: routing.md's 'Order and handoff' states 'The chosen review skill produces **findings only** — the plugin review skill states outright that applying or committing a fix is not its job', sourcing a property of the chosen (local) skill from the rejected (plugin) one. That is a sloppy citation about a shared property, not a statement that contradicts why the local skill was picked. Verdict stands as pass on the expectation as written.

expectations.text: Holds the cleanup conditional on what the review returns, because the simplifier declares it must not run on broken code - and says so in response.md
expectations.evidence: All three parts present in response.md. Grounding in the simplifier's declaration: 'The simplifier is explicit that it shouldn't run on broken code or failing tests — simplifying wrong behaviour just preserves the wrong behaviour more legibly' — which matches the plugin simplifier's description at /Users/peterkloss/Dev/ACMElabs/code-simplifier/skills/code-simplifier/SKILL.md: 'Do not use when that same code is broken or its tests are failing, since simplifying code whose behaviour is wrong preserves the wrong behaviour: fix it first.' Conditionality on review findings: 'If the review turns up actual bugs, those get fixed before the cleanup pass, not during it... So bugs first, tidying second.' Held rather than promised outright: 'I'll stop and show you the review before touching anything. "Messy" is your call, not mine — the review will separate real correctness problems from style noise, and you should pick which bucket gets cleaned.' routing.md corroborates ('So if the review turns up correctness bugs, those get fixed (or explicitly deferred) before the cleanup pass — otherwise the order inverts into a trap'), but response.md satisfies the requirement on its own.

claims.claim: The plugin code-review was not chosen because 'the user named no scope'
claims.evidence: CONTRADICTED. Plugin SKILL.md argument-hint: '[what to review: a PR ref, a branch or diff range, or a path]'; scope table: '<branch>  a branch against its merge base'. The user named a branch, which is an accepted, explicitly named scope for that skill. This is the load-bearing rejection ground and it does not hold.

claims.claim: The local code-review skill's scope model is merge-base-relative, which is what 'before I merge' means — an advantage over the plugin
claims.evidence: Half true, and misleading as a discriminator. The local skill does use three-dot diff ('git diff <fixed-point>...HEAD (three-dot, so the comparison is against the merge-base)'), but step 1 also says 'If they didn't specify one, ask for it' — it does not resolve scope itself. The plugin resolves '<branch>  a branch against its merge base' as a declared scope form. The claimed asymmetry is not real.

claims.claim: The local code-review skill's declared trigger is literally 'review a branch'
claims.evidence: Local SKILL.md description: 'Use when the user wants to review a branch, a PR, work-in-progress changes, or asks to "review since X".'

claims.claim: The chosen (local) review skill produces findings only and applies no fixes
claims.evidence: True of the local skill — its process ends at step 5 'Aggregate' with 'Present the two reports' and no edit step. But routing.md sources the claim from the wrong skill: 'the plugin review skill states outright that applying or committing a fix is not its job'. The conclusion holds; the citation is misattributed.

claims.claim: code-simplifier:code-simplifier's paired agent runs tests between changes and reverts anything that breaks them
claims.evidence: Plugin simplifier SKILL.md: 'establishes that tests pass before anything is touched, runs them after each individual change, and reverts anything that breaks them.' The agent definition code-simplifier:code-simplifier states the same.

claims.claim: The local code-simplification skill merely 'Simplifies code for clarity when refactoring' and overlaps without stating the deliverable boundary
claims.evidence: Local code-simplification SKILL.md description matches, and the file is a 331-line advisory reference with no execution/verification loop. The characterisation is accurate, though it understates the gap (advisory vs. test-verified execution) that Run A identified.

claims.claim: 'Fall back to this [the plugin] only if the personal one is unavailable'
claims.evidence: Nothing in either skill declares an availability-based precedence between them, and both are installed. This inverts the precedence stated in /Users/peterkloss/.claude/commands/code-simplify.md for the sibling collision, where the plugin is the primary and the local skill is the fallback. Peripheral to the pick's stated reason, so recorded here rather than counted separately against expectation 2 — but it points the same direction as the two load-bearing errors.

suggestions.expectation: Names both the local code-review and the plugin code-review:code-review, distinguishing which is which, and picks one rather than handing the choice back to the user
suggestions.reason: This run shows the clause working as intended but also its ceiling: the run picks decisively and is rewarded, while the pick is grounded in a false reading of the plugin's scope contract. Naming-and-picking and pick-soundness are cleanly separated across expectations 1 and 2, which is good design — worth keeping, but the eval report should not read expectation 1 alone as evidence the collision was handled well.

No expectation names the specific trap. Both runs face the same fork, and the whole difference between them is whether they believe the plugin can take a bare branch as scope. An expectation reading 'does not reject the plugin on the ground that no scope was named, since a branch is an accepted scope form for it' would be sharply discriminating and would not depend on the grader being briefed with the right files to open.

suggestions.expectation: The stated reason for the pick is not contradicted elsewhere in the same outputs
suggestions.reason: Passes here for a run whose reasoning is externally wrong, confirming it measures coherence rather than correctness. It also missed a genuine defect in this run — routing.md attributes the chosen local skill's findings-only property to the rejected plugin skill. Broadening it to 'no property claimed for the chosen skill is sourced from a different skill' would let it catch cross-file attribution drift without duplicating expectation 2.

Expectation 4 passed for both runs, so it did not discriminate on this pair. That is not a defect — it is a real safety property and worth keeping as a floor — but the eval author should know it currently carries no signal about whether the skill under test helped.

eval_feedback.overall: The set correctly separates 'did it pick' from 'was the pick sound', and expectation 2 is what caught this run's real failure. Its dependence on the grader knowing which installed files to open is the main fragility; naming the branch-is-a-scope fact in the expectation itself would fix that.
